label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
**4 out of 5 stars — a worthwhile improvement, with a few things to know**

We paid $2,140 for the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 from Chancel AV in February 2026, plus $95 for the wall mount. For our congregation, that was a substantial purchase. We had been livestreaming worship with a webcam since 2020, and I wanted something better for the people watching at home without buying more camera than we needed. After several months of use, I would buy it again, though I don’t think every small church needs to spend this much.

Our nave is 92 feet long, and the camera is mounted on the balcony rail at the back. The 20x optical zoom makes that distance workable in a way the webcam never did. The picture is much clearer, especially when we move from a wide view to the pulpit or lectern. Delores, who is 82 and homebound, called to tell me she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That meant more to me than the specifications on the box.

For those comparing connections, it offers 1080p60, NDI HX and ordinary HDMI output. Power over Ethernet lets us run one cable up to the balcony, which was a real advantage for our installation. We still use OBS on the old office PC and stream to YouTube, usually for 30–60 viewers on a Sunday. Buying this camera did not require us to replace the whole arrangement.

We have nine presets saved: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide view, and two views of the chancel steps. Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, learned to operate it from the free web app on a tablet in one afternoon. Once things were set up, regular Sunday operation was quite manageable.

Getting there took some patience. The manual is thin and badly translated. I am a pastor, not an engineer, and there were places where I needed more explanation than it supplied. Marcy at Chancel AV was excellent on the phone and helped make up for the shortcomings of the printed instructions.

We also had an unsettling first Sunday: by the sermon, the presets had drifted a few degrees from where we had saved them. The March firmware update, version 2.4, fixed that for us. Autofocus is another limitation. If someone walks between the camera and the pulpit, it can hunt for focus. We now lock focus on the presets rather than leave it to decide during worship.

Low-light performance is better than our old webcam, but it is not miraculous. At our Easter Vigil in April, during the first “Christ the Lord Is Risen Today,” we had only candlelight. The picture became grainy, but it remained usable. The old webcam would have shown little besides dots of light. Don’t expect a bright, crisp picture in those conditions, but we could actually share the service.

One important warning: this did nothing for our sound problem. Audio is not the camera’s job. If people cannot hear your readers or understand the sermon, budget and plan for that separately.

My rating is **4 out of 5 stars**. It has made a meaningful difference for our homebound members and others joining us online. Still, a congregation under 100 might do perfectly well with something cheaper. Consider your distance, lighting and actual needs before spending the money. For our long nave and balcony position, it has been worth it.
